Meta is showing off its AI-powered Ray-Bans, Salesforce and GoDaddy are promoting their AI tools, and Google had a major ad queued up for Workspace, but [had to remake it](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2j15r1g09o) because its cheese fact was wrong.

Who’s behind this move? None other than Kate Rouch, the company’s [new CMO](https://www.adweek.com/brand-marketing/openai-finds-its-first-cmo-in-ex-coinbase-marketing-chief-kate-rouch/) and the ex-CMO of Coinbase back when it launched its own [viral Super Bowl ad](https://youtu.be/uJ9pNQrz0fA?feature=shared) during [The Crypto Bowl](https://www.businessinsider.com/look-back-crypto-bowl-super-bowl-ads-2023-1) of 2022.

Sam’s already cryptically teasing the spot ([x.com](https://x.com/sama/status/1887679355112837201)) with emoji riddles about a “Superb Owl.” _Soo… should we expect a big announcement… or just another QR code?_

As we’ve [said before](https://www.theneurondaily.com/p/ai-aces-math-olympics), Super Bowls (and other major sporting events) are great measures for where [we are in the hype-cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gartner_hype_cycle)… _let’s just hope 2025 doesn’t end the same way _[_as 2022_](https://www.npr.org/2022/12/29/1145297807/crypto-crash-ftx-cryptocurrency-bitcoin)_… _

# Here’s the top 13 insights from Andrej Karpathy’s epic, 3-hour AI explainer… 

Youtube: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (https://youtu.be/7xTGNNLPyMI?feature=shared)

Yesterday, we shared Andrej Karpathy's [mind-blowing 3+ hour video](https://youtu.be/7xTGNNLPyMI?feature=shared) breaking down how ChatGPT and other AI models work—from digesting internet data to “reasoning.”

**Why should you care?** Well, Karpathy isn't just any AI researcher. He was employee #4 at OpenAI, ran Tesla's AI division, and is known for making complex AI concepts digestible for normal humans (_including you, Mom_).

**Want to learn all about AI, but don’t have 3 hours to kill? Here are 10 key insights: **

1. **Pre-training Data **([00:01:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=60s)): All AI requires training data, and they get this data from the internet; this [internet data](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1) goes through extensive filtering—removing spam, adult content, and personal information—resulting in ~44 terabytes of high-quality text the models learn from.

2. **Tokenization** ([00:07:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=467s)): Language models break text into “tokens” rather than characters. You can think of them like puzzle pieces for words. GPT-4 uses ~100,277 of these pieces to put together its responses. 

3. **Neural Network I/O** ([00:14:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=867s)): Models predict one token at a time, based on previous tokens, with a finite amount of computation possible for each prediction.

4. **GPT-2 Training **([00:31:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=1869s)): Training costs plummeted from $40K (2019) to as low as ~$100 today thanks to optimization. **Fun fact: **Karpathy trains a GPT-2 model live during the video. _Wild!_

5. **Base Model Inference** ([00:42:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=2572s)): Base models come first, and act as “internet simulators,” generating text that matches patterns they've seen—but they aren't assistants.

6. **Post-training Data** ([01:01:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=3666s)): Models learn to be assistants through what’s called “supervised fine-tuning”, using conversation data that’s both human-created and synthetically generated.

7. **Knowledge & Memory** ([01:20:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=4832s)): Language models have two types of memory: _parameters_ (like vague childhood memories) and the _context window_ (like having a book open right in front of you). This is also why they hallucinate…it’s like when you’re pretty sure you remember something, but you’re actually mixing up different memories.

8. **Model Thinking** ([01:46:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=6416s)): Models need multiple tokens to process complex thoughts—they can't solve difficult problems in a single step—hence the effectiveness of “chain of thought” prompting (“go step by step”).

9. **DeepSeek-R1** ([02:27:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=8867s)): Karpathy demonstrates how advanced models (like o3, Flash Thinking, and of course R1) do “explicit reasoning”, showing their work and checking answers from multiple angles.

10. **RLHF** ([02:48:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=10106s)): Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) helps improve model outputs, but has limitations since it relies on simulated, rather than real, human feedback.

**Here's what Karpathy says we should ****[expect next](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=11379s)****:** 

* Language models are evolving toward _true_ multimodality—seamlessly handling text, audio, and images together. 

* They'll also become more independent, handling longer-running tasks (like [Operator does](https://www.theneurondaily.com/p/operator-book-me-some-clients)) with human oversight. 

* The challenge now lies in developing [test-time training](https://techcrunch.com/2024/07/17/ttt-models-might-be-the-next-frontier-in-generative-ai/) so models can learn from new experiences like humans do, especially when dealing with extremely long contexts in multimodal interactions.

Karpathy emphasizes treating AI as a powerful but imperfect tool—great for inspiration and first drafts, but still requires human verification and ownership of the final product.

# Prompt Tip of the Day

Want to master o1 and o3-mini? Microsoft's [latest research](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azure-ai-services-blog/prompt-engineering-for-openai%E2%80%99s-o1-and-o3-mini-reasoning-models/4374010) says instead of the usual GPT tricks (examples, step-by-step guides, chain-of-thought), these models need the opposite approach: crystal-clear context and minimal instructions.

**Give them: **

1. The essential facts/context they need (_they don't know everything!_). 

2. A clear statement of what you want. 

3. Your desired output format.

Then, step back and let their built-in reasoning engine work. These models crush complex tasks when you keep prompts clean and skip the usual GPT engineering. Simple = smarter! 

Speaking of _smarter_, we had o1-pro synthesize all that advice and build a [custom prompt template](https://chatgpt.com/share/67a55ff2-7b1c-8003-abf5-bac5e18fa38a) out of it ([pastebin version](https://pastebin.com/stdxRj8h))—enjoy!

# Intelligent Insights

* The Algorithmic Bridge [argues](https://www.thealgorithmicbridge.com/p/agi-is-already-hereits-just-not-evenly) as AI gets more powerful (like OpenAI's [Deep Research](https://openai.com/index/introducing-deep-research/)), the gap between basic and expert users actually grows larger—meaning your ability to craft good prompts could be the difference between getting mediocre results and PhD-level analysis. 

* Here’s a fantastic article from Ethan Mollick about what [deep research](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/p/the-end-of-search-the-beginning-of) means for the world. 

* This [visual guide](https://newsletter.maartengrootendorst.com/p/a-visual-guide-to-reasoning-llms) to reasoning models is great for understanding how they work.  

* Stanford + University of Washington researchers built an OpenAI competitor [for just $50](https://sherwood.news/tech/ai-researchers-trained-an-openai-competitor-in-26-minutes-for-less-than/) and in ~26 minutes by creatively using “wait” commands to improve the model's reasoning ([paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.19393))—they distilled it from [Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-2.0-flash-thinking-exp-01-21), btw. _Nobody tell the market, you saw what they did _[_after DeepSeek!_](https://www.theneurondaily.com/p/monday-s-ai-crash-explained)
